utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-08-91-T, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Good morning to everyone. May we have the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Alex Demirdjian with Belinda Pidwell and Sebastiaan van Hooydonk for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Appearing for Stanisic, Slobodan Cvijetic, Ms. Montgomery, and our intern Annemarie McNulty.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Dragan Krgovic, Aleksandar Aleksic, and Miroslav Cuskic appearing for Zupljanin Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Before the witness is escorted back to the stand, continuing where we left off yesterday with counsel's estimate of the time that would be required to complete this witness's testimony and the optimistic result that we would get to Witness -- the next witness on Friday, thank you, Witness number 20. Mr. Krgovic, your proofing notes should be supplied by close of business today.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll do my best, Your Honours. Since he is a character witness who is arriving today in The Hague, I will see him around 12.00, and after that I will be able to submit my proofing notes from that interview. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. And if there is nothing else to delay us, would the usher please escort the witness back to the stand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And before I invite Mr. Krgovic to begin, I remind you of the solemn declaration that you made yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krgovic -- Mr. Aleksic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Bubic.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD BUBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Yesterday, at the end of the working day, you provided some basic information about yourself, and now I would kindly ask you to fill in the information with some detail. Tell us something about your educational background. What schools did you complete, when, and where?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD BUBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I completed the elementary school in the village where I was born, and after that I attended school in Zagreb. In Zagreb, I completed secondary military technical school. At the end of my education, I became an active non-commissioned officer. After that, I spent some time working for the JNA as an active-duty officer. Do you need anything else?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: I have to wait for the transcript. We have to make pauses between your answers and my questions, and vice versa. Everything is fine. We just have to be mindful of the transcript. Tell me, where did you serve as an officer in the JNA and for how long?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD BUBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From 1966 to 1972, for the most part in the territory of Istria in Pula, Rijeka, Umag and Pazin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: And after that, when you stopped serving in the JNA, where did you live and what did you do?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD BUBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I returned to Kotor Varos, and there I found employment in a company in the sales department. And then in 1985 I became a businessman. I had a chain of boutiques and I was involved in that up until the beginning of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Just briefly - and we will come back to that in the course of your testimony - after the war broke out, what happened to you? What was your destiny throughout the entire war?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD BUBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was engaged in the Territorial Defence of the city of Kotor Varos. On the eve of the day when the conflict broke out, I was engaged. And then I was captured by the BiH army and the HVO and I spent some time in prison. When I was released, unfortunately I had to undergo medical treatment, and after that I continued working in the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: After you were set free until 1992, which unit did you belong to, to what company?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD BUBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I received my call-up papers, I reported to the command of the town defence and I worked in a local company in the territory of the town of Kotor Varos. We were deployed as guards. Our task was to prevent any sort of attack. And I stayed in that position until the moment I was captured and I was arrested.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: We will come back to that as well. I asked you when you were exchanged, when you were set free after you recovered. After that, in the course of 1992, where were you?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD BUBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was still in Kotor Varos. I still stood guard. Better to say, I was in the immediate vicinity of the building where I resided.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: And later, during the war in 1993, 1994, 1995, did you stay in the same position? Did you change your unit?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD BUBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I stayed with the same unit. When the Kotor Varos brigade was established, its name was light assault brigade Kotor Varos. Because of the trauma that I had suffered and my health status, I was transferred to become a member of the logistics base with the command of the light assault brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Tell me, when the war ended - you have told us what your profession is now - but let me ask you what was your profession between 1995 to 1997?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD BUBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From 1995, i.e., from the end of the war, until 2004, I was unemployed. I didn't have a job. I didn't work. As -- and then I started working for the NGO, the association of inmates of the VRS, and I'm still the secretary-general of that association.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: And do you have contacts with some other NGOs, some other organisations? Can you provide some detail?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD BUBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have contacts with a huge number of other NGOs across Bosnia and Herzegovina, irrespective of the fact whether they belonged to the Croatian, Serbian, or Muslim peoples. A lot of my work implies working with some international organisations. I can say without any false modesty that I'm very active. In the NDPCRS [as interpreted] there is a Swiss NGO. It's on the tip of my tongue, but I really can't remember its name. I also co-operate with the association of inmates of Bosnia and Herzegovina. That is a federal organisation. And also with the Muslim Federation of inmates in the territory of Western Bosnia with headquarters in Kladusa. We are all involved in that work, especially through UNDP. We are involved in the process leading to establishing the process of transitional justice in Bosnia-Herzegovina. And this concerns the entire system of justice in all of its elements, and we are particularly engaged in bringing justice to the victims of the last war.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Were you ever a member of any political party?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD BUBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a time when I was a member of the League of Communists in the former Yugoslavia. After that, I have never been engaged in any party, in any political party. I'm talking about mono-ethnic parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Do you know Mr. Stojan Zupljanin?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD BUBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I know him. We were born in the same village. We even went to school together for a while. He's three years younger than me so we know each other from very early childhood.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: In the course of 1992, did you have any contacts with Mr. Stojan Zupljanin?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD BUBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be very specific, in 1992 I don't think I had any contacts. Later on, I saw him in the village where we were born, in Maslovare. He was bringing back either his mother or his father - I'm not sure, actually - from hospital or from a medical examination, something of the kind. I can't be very precise and provide you any more specific details.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: When Mr. -- since Mr. Stojan Zupljanin has been here in The Hague, have you had any personal contacts with him?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD BUBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Do you remember when the Defence team for Mr. Stojan Zupljanin contacted you the first time, and who was it who got in touch with you?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD BUBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I got a telephone call from Mr. Drago Vukelic from Banja Luka. He told me that he was a member of the Zupljanin Defence team, and he asked me if I would be willing to come and appear before the Tribunal to testify what I know about Stojan and the circumstances that surrounded some of the events, and I agreed without any second thoughts. Sometime at the beginning --

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD BUBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was last summer. And then during the summer of this year they called me again and asked me, or rather, I agreed to testify and then they called me into their office to take a statement, to take notes, and to get my signed consent. And on that occasion, they told me that the Prosecutor also wanted to talk to me. And I asked those people how customary was that, to talk to both sides? I was interested in how things were done until then and I was told that very few people talked to both sides. And it was then that I refused to talk to the representatives of the OTP. We were supposed to meet sometime during the summer of this year and then we would have to sign an official agreement. Unfortunately, I became ill and I had to spend two months in bed. And then we met again sometime in early October. Then I signed my statement again and I confirmed that I was willing to testify on behalf of the Defence, that I was only willing to talk to the Defence team, nobody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Besides Mr. Vukelic, have you had contacts with any other members of the Stojan Zupljanin Defence team?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD BUBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A few months ago, I met Mr. Krgovic and yourself.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: And did you speak to me eyeball to eyeball at any time and when?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD BUBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, actually, we never spoke the two of us alone. We spoke in the presence of Mr. Vukelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: When you arrived here in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD BUBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I beg your pardon?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: When you arrived in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD BUBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spent a couple of days with you and we discussed all sorts of things.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Very well. And now could you please tell us how much you remember. It was a long time ago. What was the political climate and the security situation in Kotor Varos and the general area in the spring of 1992, just briefly what you can remember?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD BUBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When a multi-party system came onto the scene, that was the beginning of the state of anarchy in the municipality. Mono-ethnic parties were established. The first one was the Croatian party, the HDZ; after that, the Muslim SDA; and finally, the Serbian Democratic Party. There were huge rallies where you could hear stories about the doom and gloom if the others came to the power. And people were terrified, to put it simply. In the meantime, the leaders of those parties invited people to slowly prepare for war. People started arming themselves. Weapons arrived through God knows what channels -- from all over the place. A huge number of people bought weapons. Some of them paid the last penny. Some of them sold their only cow to buy weapons, but in any case weapons they did buy. There came a time when they started walking around the town brandishing those weapons, especially when a unit arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: You said that people started walking about armed. Which people were those? To which ethnicity did they belong?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD BUBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was everybody, more or less. A division was -- became obvious in the town. It first began in pubs. Croats went to one pub or some pubs and Serbs to others, and so on. And sometimes there were groups of trouble-makers who deliberately went to the meeting-places of the other ethnicity to create mayhem. And the security situation was very bad.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Talking about the villages in the area, tell us about their ethnic composition and their geographic position of the villages around Kotor Varos.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD BUBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Kotor Varos itself is in a beautiful valley of the Vrbanja river. There are rolling hills and the town itself had a mixed population, people from all ethnicities. But many villages around town were mono-ethnic. You can call them that, I think. There were very few villages that were ethnically mixed. But even so, some ethnic groups would be -- would constitute a minority in such villages. And this general security, it was the Muslim forces which, as soon as May 1992, began to erect barricades on the roads. They prohibited people from passing. In the village of Vrbanjci which is 5 or 6 kilometres from Kotor Varos, some century-old trees were cut down to block the roads and the situation was by no means good.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: You spoke about people arming themselves. Were the villages armed, too, were there village guards?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD BUBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time there was no difference between the town and the villages. The villagers, too, began arming themselves, and in May I believe there was no one village left in the municipality without armed village guards.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: You mentioned a minute ago that a military unit arrived. Which unit was that and what do you know about it or what did you know about it?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD BUBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a unit of the JNA, the 22nd Brigade. But it wasn't a whole brigade that came to Kotor Varos municipality. As far as I know, only one battalion arrived. And the command of that battalion was at Maslovare village and the army had its camp at Borije in the Kruscica river valley. The commander of that unit was a certain Colonel Peulic. And later, when the armed attacks in the municipality began, the unit, including its command, was relocated to Vrbanjci which is 5 or 6 kilometres from the place that I mentioned as being the first one where barricades were put up. As far as I knew, the task of the unit was to protect the people from armed attacks and to prevent possible incidents involving the use of fire-arms.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Did those soldiers come to town occasional and how did they conduct themselves? What happened when they were there?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD BUBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, soldiers will be soldiers. They will come to town and they were armed, and there was shooting sometimes in front of pubs or on the streets. There will be drunken people, all sorts of folks, and clearly the local population was even more afraid and insecure.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: You mentioned Colonel Peulic. Did you learn what his function and role was in the area?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD BUBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Initially, he was the commander of the 22nd Brigade and, as far as I know, he later became -- he became the Commander-in-Chief for the general area. I think it extended to the Vlasic mountain plateau. And I dare say that he was the man who was the master of life and death there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Did you see him in Kotor Varos in June and later; that is, before you were taken prisoner and after you were released?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD BUBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I met him occasionally. I didn't know the man personally, but I saw him around. He did used to come to Kotor Varos, especially after my release.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Tell us something about the events from -- that happened in early June in Kotor Varos and around town.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD BUBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The village guards and the surrounding villages in Kotor Varos municipality were gradually evolving into armed units so that, more or less, each village had its mini armed unit which was mono-ethnic. When I say "mono-ethnic," well, I must add that there were villages where people were on good terms and the units comprised Croats, Serbs, and Muslims. But there was talk all over the place that strong forces were being formed in the area around Kotor Varos, at least that was the story that we Serbs heard, and that those forces were to attack Kotor Varos. I believe that this will be discussed later on. There was some information that a forceful military action was planned to destroy prominent Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: What did you learn about this? Can you tell us some more?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD BUBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was during my captivity that I heard most about it. A certain Stipo Maric, also known as Sprzo, told me that the Croats and Muslims were to unite on the 12th of May, if I'm not mistaken, to organise a hunting lunch on Mount Borije, and they wanted to invite all prominent Serbs and there were lists for liquidation. Whether or not that's true, I don't know, because I've never seen a document. But there was public talk about it in Kotor Varos. We know that groups of those mono-ethnic, armies to call them that, on both banks of the Vrbanja river were gaining ground and growing.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: You said on the 12th of May or that's how it was recorded. Was that the date of that hunting lunch?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD BUBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, I'm sorry, I meant June.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything about the events at Vasiljevic Brdo, or Vrbanjci at that time?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD BUBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those paramilitary units that were established and were not part of the TO began to kill people. At Vasiljevic Brdo, around the 1st, I think, but I cannot be sure of the date, a man was killed. At Vagani village, an old man - I believe he was over 75 - was killed. I can't recall his name now. But he was minding his sheep and some Croats and Muslims came and asked him to give them some lambs. He refused and they simply killed him. In the direction of Bilice village, when you go from Kotor Varos, there was a killing. A man called a soldier -- he called out to him, probably he wanted to say something to him or wanted him to come over, and the soldier replied by -- with a burst of fire, killing him. And I believe that was the first killing in Kotor Varos.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: For the clarity of the record, these victims at Vasiljevica Brdo and -- just a second, and Vagani, what was the ethnicity of those victims?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD BUBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: And the first killing in town, do you know the ethnicity of the victim?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD BUBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A Serb, too. I even knew him personally. His name was Nedjo Eskic. He was the director of a catering company in Kotor Varos. He was a relatively young man.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Who were the perpetrators, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD BUBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Nedjo's case, they were Croats. They had come from Bilice village.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: As far as you personally are concerned, did anything happen to you in early June? What was your status?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD BUBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I responded to the call-up, like the majority of the citizens of Kotor Varos, not only Serbs but Croats and Muslims too. I was standing guard in front of two or three buildings there, or actually, I was the guard commander. But then the guards in town were abolished and moved to the suburbs to prevent the extremist forces from entering town. And I was at a position outside town which was on a hill called Ruji Da.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Or some such. The interpreter didn't catch the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Can you repeat the name of the hill.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD BUBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Rujika.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: You said you were mobilised. Who handed you the call-up document and tell us more about the technical aspect?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD BUBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I received a summons from the defence secretariat to join the TO staff and report at the town command of Kotor Varos. It was some 300 or 400 metres from the place I lived. I was to report to Captain Gojko Stolic. He was an acquaintance of mine. I had known him long. He told me that I would be beside the buildings for a while and he showed me where with a gesture of his hand. And he said that guards would be deployed on Rujika hill.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Did he have a rank?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD BUBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a reserve captain.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: What was the establishment unit that was mobilised then as part of the TO?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD BUBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The unit was called the TO company, and according to my modest acquaintance with the rules of military engagement, it had about 120 men. The company commander was Gojko Stolic. Its headquarters was at a pub which was called X.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: It was the town company of Kotor Varos TO. Do you know whether in the surrounding villages there was such companies as well and if they were mobilised?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD BUBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether there were any companies because I didn't go to those villages, but, as far as the Serbian army is concerned, each and every unit was called a company. Now, whether that was technically correct, I don't know. But they had their company commanders and their platoon commanders, but how strong they were in terms of manpower, I don't know. But each village had its company and that includes Serb villages and the villages populated by the other two peoples in Kotor Varos municipality. If I may add, at Bilice village, as far as I know, larger units began to rally. Bilice is on the right bank of the Vrbanja, and at Hadrovci village larger groups of Croats and Muslims were formed. I know that those units were commanded by a certain Sadikovic. I don't know when exactly, but before the war he was appointed commander of the Kotor Varos police station on ethnic grounds.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Did you know how strong the units at Bilice and Hadrovci were?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD BUBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't at the time, but when I was taken prisoner I had the opportunity to make an estimate. And I think that they were rather strong. There were rumours that at Bilice there were over 500 men at arms, and since I was a prisoner on the left bank of the Vrbanja -- there were a couple hundred of men where I was being held too.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: We'll get back to that when we begin to discuss your captivity. You said that members -- that people of all three ethnicities responded to the call-up?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD BUBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Do you know if a number of Croats and Muslims remained in the units of the TO which later became the VRS?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD BUBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite a number of both Croats and Muslims remained in those units. They were peace-loving people who were not in favour of war. Also, quite a number were mobilised. They wanted to do that because they wanted to get hold of weapons. And then, when they got hold of weapons, they would join their mono-ethnic units in their villages. There was a number of people who, when the company became a brigade, remained in the unit and followed the war path of that unit until the end of the war. For example, a good friend of mine - who is still my friend - Asim Aganbegovic, who worked in the Territorial Defence staff before the war and even was our battalion commander during the war, he's a Muslim. I can't remember anybody else, but I believe that Adis Hadziselimovic was also one of the commanders in our brigade during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: We will come back to those names a bit later. I will remind you of some of them. You mentioned Captain Stolic and you've told us where the command of the town was. Do you know where the secretariat for National Defence was before the war, in what building?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD BUBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. A modern building was erected quite some time before the war and it has the police station on the ground floor, and then on the first floor, there was the department of the Ministry of Defence, i.e., the Territorial Defence staff of the town of Kotor Varos. And the name of that body was secretariat, and the chief of that secretariat was Manojlo Tepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: After the war broke out in Kotor Varos municipality, did Mr. Manojlo Tepic remain in that position or did he perhaps change his position afterwards? What do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD BUBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, he spent the entire time in the secretariat. When the brigade was established, he had a short stint in the brigade command but I don't know at what position. After that as a brigade member he was there until the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: You mentioned a moment when the brigade was established. What brigade do you have in mind when you say that?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD BUBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Kotor Varos light brigade. According to some Territorial Defence rules, I suppose, before the war every village or town had a war establishment of the size of a light brigade; Banja Luka had several, Laktasi had one, Gradiste had one, likewise Kotor Varos also established its own brigade. I believe that that was sometime in late June, or thereabouts, or perhaps in early July, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Who were the members of that brigade? Was that a town brigade and did only the companies from the town enter the composition of the brigade or anybody else, for example, from the villages?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD BUBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that troops from the entire territory of the Kotor Varos municipality became members of the brigade, leaving only a minimum number of men to stand guard in the villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Do you know who the commander of that brigade was, the Kotor Varos light brigade?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD BUBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The commander of that brigade was Lieutenant-Colonel Dusan Novakovic. He is from Banja Luka. I met him for the first time when I returned from the detention camp. That was sometime in late July or possibly in early August. I can't remember when that was for a fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Was he an active-duty officer?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD BUBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was an active-duty officer. He was a lieutenant-colonel of the JNA. He had arrived from the corps pursuant to an order, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: At the time when you were mobilised and when the entire composition of the Territorial Defence of Kotor Varos was mobilised, do you know if any other forces were mobilised; and if that was the case, what forces were those?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD BUBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The police station was brought up to strength. Reserve officers were mobilised to reinforce the police station. I don't know what their establishment numerical strength was supposed to be, but I know that a lot of people from the reserve police force were called up and that they became members of the police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: OBRAD BUBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would also like to mention that reserve policemen who were called up were not only Serbs but also non-Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Do you know if any of those reserve police officers stayed as members of the active police force?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD BUBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have a neighbour who lives in the next-door building. His name is Sejdo Tatar. He was active all the time. He fought on the side of our army. And also, in my neighbourhood, not far from where I live, there is another person called Asim Arnautovic. He still lives at the same address in Kotor Varos. There are quite a few other, but I can't remember their names.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: You have told us that in the month of June the town was split, that it was divided. Can you tell us more about that in geographical terms. Who was it who kept what side of the town?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD BUBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the right bank of the river Vrbanja, there was strong forces of the Territorial Defence involving all three ethnic groups. The control was in the hand of the Serbs. And on the left bank of the Vrbanja, that side was under the control of Muslims in concert with Croats. But their numbers were smaller. There were fewer Croats than Muslims. Apparently there was an agreement with the National Defence structures, according to which one of the largest Croatian villages with a majority Croatian population Zabrdje, Sibovi, Novo Selo, would not participate in any combat. As a result of that, at the beginning of war, they surrendered their weapons and those villages down there remained unperturbed throughout the war. On the right bank of the Vrbanja river, however, some 5 or 6 kilometres from Kotor Varos, Muslim and Croat units started forming and the main role in that was played by a certain Muhamed Sadikovic. I have already mentioned that before the war he was appointed as the commander of the police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: As far as the old town is concerned -- or rather, the old fortress in the town, were there any troops there? Were there any units there?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD BUBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was personally there for a couple of days. After I was captured, I was taken there. This is an elevation from which you could control the town with weapons. I'm not an expert in weaponry or military tactics, but this is my assumption. The entire territory of the town could be observed from that elevation. You're talking about a medieval fortress or a fort which was built by Hrvoje Vukcic. There was quite a big military unit there composed of Muslims and Croats. It was of a mixed composition.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, just for clarification, could you tell us exactly when you were captured and where you were held and for how long.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I was captured on the 5th of July, 1992, in a place called Rujevica which is some 3 or 4 kilometres away from Kotor Varos on the Banja Luka-Teslic road. I was taken to the left bank of the Vrbanja river, where I spent 15 days. During that time, I was at several places, but most of the time I spent in a kiln for dry-curing meat, and the size of that kiln was 1 metre by 2. Would you like to know anything else?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Were you held with other detainees during your captivity or were you in a single cell?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All the time I was by myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And, finally, was the medical treatment that you had to undergo after you were released, was that related to your captivity? In other words, sir, were you mistreated during your captivity to such an extent that you needed medical treatment afterwards?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. There was a lot of mistreatment going on, too much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. And may I add on behalf of the Chamber that of course we wish to express our empathy with the suffering that you had to go through.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I was going to put a few questions to the witness about the detention and what he learned during the detention, but I will leave that for after the break because there is something I'd like to tackle before the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bubic, you mentioned the fact that some people voluntarily surrendered their weapons. Do you know anything about that activity, about the negotiations leading to that result? What do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD BUBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A majority of the population of Kotor Varos - and I mean all three ethnic groups - were against the war, and that's a fact. However, there was also a number of those who, for whatever reason, were not bothered by the prospect of fighting. I'm sure that the Serbian side did not want a war. And when the Serbian authorities were established in Kotor Varos, and that was sometime in the first decade [as interpreted] of the month of June 1992, delegations started touring the surrounding villages to talk with the prominent figures in those villages about the surrender of weapons. Prominent Muslims were involved in those negotiations, religious officials, hodzas, even Catholic priests were members of those delegations, as well as representatives of the army. They promised that they would absolutely protect the population if they decided to return weapons. Those negotiations took place in Kotor, in the village on the left bank of the Vrbanja, with the majority Muslim Croat population. And negotiations also took place in Zabrdje with a majority Croatian population. Negotiations were also held in Vrbanjci, to be more precise in Vecici and Garici which is a place near to my Maslovare, also in Siprage which is a village bordering on the municipality of Travnik which was inhabited by Muslims. But people will be people, as you know. The village of Zabrdje, for example, which had quite a number of inhabitants, I can't tell you exactly how many, people returned weapons, and during the war I believe that they had only one incident when a child was killed. And that child was killed by an extremist, a Croat, and that girl was taken in an ambulance, in our ambulance, to Banja Luka. But she was killed on the way by a member of her own people. So in that village there were no casualties. As for the village of Garici near my village of Maslovare, where I was born, the population there also returned weapons, and I believe that they did not have a single casualty during the war. Nobody was killed there. The village of Siprage, bordering on the municipality of Travnik, as I've already told you, the population there voluntarily surrendered their weapons. The villagers remained living there throughout the war and the village still lives a life that I can't describe as normal because there is no normal life anywhere in Kotor Varos or in any other surrounding village. The village of Vecici was a stronghold of Muslims on the left bank of the Vrbanja in the territory of the local commune of Vrbanjci. I'm sure that there were five or six rounds of negotiations with that village. They were hard-liners, they were stubborn, and they said: No, we don't want to surrender our weapons at the expense of war, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, just a small intervention for the transcript. At page 20, line 15, the witness says: "The Serbian authorities were established in Kotor Varos, and that was sometime in the first decade of the month of June 1992 ..." Can we just clarify with the witness when he says that the Serbian authorities were established in Kotor Varos. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Could you please repeat for the record what you meant when you spoke about the Serbs establishing the authorities in Kotor Varos.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD BUBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that it was on the 10th or the 11th of June, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you one more thing before the break. Are you familiar with the combat activities in Vecici from late June 1992? Do you know what happened at Vecici then?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD BUBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I do. And it was due to that that I was taken prisoner. They didn't want to surrender their weapons voluntarily. Then the army began to march on Vecici. It was toward the end of June, not sure about the date. They were met by well-armed Muslims, and I think that about two dozen of our men were killed, soldiers and police officers, because the police was in co-ordinated action with the army and under military command. Due to such heavy losses, our forces withdrew to their initial positions. They were unable to recover the dead and the wounded, if there were any, which we didn't know. It only happened some five or six days later due to talks whether people or who had some common sense left and they were buried on the 5th of July, I mean those killed. I was at a burial one day and that's when I was taken prisoner.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: We'll speak some more about that after the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think that this is a convenient time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So we take the break to return in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bubic, let's go back to what we discussed before the break. You said that a large number of soldiers and police officers was killed during the combat at Vecici. Do you know whether any soldiers or police officers were taken prisoner and what their fate was?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD BUBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were some who were taken prisoner, but unfortunately they returned in body bags. They were killed subsequently. What's more, they were monstrously mistreated. Some were scorched with welding kits and some people say that they heard their screams. Maybe this added to the already existing chaos, to distrust, to contemplations of revenge and so on. It was madness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: You began to describe what happened to you in early July. Could you please continue in chronological order. You mentioned the 5th of July, so let's take it from there.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD BUBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 4th of July, I learned that on the following day all those who had fallen in battle would be buried at -- or rather, who had fallen at battle in Vecici would be buried. Three lads were from the immediate vicinity of my weekend cottage. I went to see the commander of the company to which I belonged, Gojko Stolic, and said to him that it wouldn't be a bad thing for me to go to the burial of those lads on the next day. And it would also be an excellent opportunity for me to go and see my wife and daughter who were staying at Maslovare, my birthplace. Mr. Stolic replied that there were no problems and that I could go. I set off on that same evening and he gave me a permit, because otherwise you couldn't leave the unit. So I had this permit to leave the unit and I went home in the evening. I prepared for my departure on the following day and I left rather early because there was no public transportation along the road to Teslic. Instead, we would hitch a ride with whoever passed by because the distance is 18 kilometres, after all. There was a truck that was transporting probably food for the soldiers, and I hitched a ride on that truck. We spoke. I saw my immediate family. And then I returned in the same way. I went as far as Donji Obodnik, where the three killed men were to be buried. I was present at the burial which just barely took place because from the left bank of the Vrbanja they began shooting at us from sniping rifles. And then we would hide behind tombstones at the graveyard. But then the burial did take place. A couple of grenades were fired from tanks on the Serb side in the direction of the place from where the sniping had come and then the burial took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Please hold on a moment. Mr. Bubic, I know that this is difficult for you to re-live all this once more, but on the other hand I understand that you feel the need to give us an account of all these details. But do tell us whom you met on your way to the cemetery and what happened later.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD BUBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were no more than about 50 people at the burial of these three young men. I met Mr. Petrusic who is also from Maslovare and he had work obligation in Kotor Varos. He's a driver by profession. When we reached Vrbanjci he told me when he had to report at his unit -- actually, he wasn't with a unit, he had to report at his work-place, and I told him when I had to report at my unit. And then we agreed that since he had to leave before me and he had a free seat -- but if -- and that would -- we would rather ride a vehicle -- on a vehicle which had two free seats. And then a truck arrived from the neighbouring village. Down there, there were quite a few people who were waiting for transportation either to Maslovare or to Kotor Varos. Most people were going up.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Did you see anybody there?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD BUBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw many people there, many people I knew. Among others, there was also the then-municipal president of Kotor Varos, Nedeljko Djekanovic. I met the commander of the police station of Maslovare, Nedeljko Bubic, who was even a distant relative of mine. We commented a bit because on that day there -- the Serbian army attacked the fortifications at Vecici from the air. And you know how it is at war time. We were goofing and spoofing, and I made a joke about how good it would be to level the hills toward river there and I said, "I'll build a catering facility there and make good money." So we were, you know, fooling around. But then from the direction of Vecici, Zdravko Pejic arrived, who at the time worked at the police station; he was accompanied by Hamid Bajric, yes, it was him; a hodza from Kotor Varos whose name I don't know; and I think that a priest was there from the Catholic church at Vrbanjci. I heard from them that they were going to talks to put an end to this madness, for people to disarm themselves, and normal life to start again. After that we were constantly looking around, whether anybody would come along. There were some vehicles going to Kotor Varos, but they either didn't want to or didn't dare pick us up. They said either that they weren't going down or that somebody was waiting for them further down the road. And after an hour, an hour and a half, an Opel Omega arrived and two uniformed persons stepped out. I approached them and asked them whether they were going to Kotor Varos. They said, "Yes." "Could the two of us ride with you?" He -- and they replied, "No problem. We just have a meeting at the command." There was Peulic and somebody else, I don't remember. We sat down and it didn't take long, maybe 15 to 20 minutes, until we set off for Kotor Varos. Since I had travelled the same -- along the same road before in a Golf, I was shot at in a bend. Luckily I wasn't hurt. But, based on that experience, I suggested to the driver - and only later did I learn that it was a police colonel or a lieutenant-colonel by the name of Stevilovic - to step on it and to drive faster because they sometimes shoot at -- shoot at vehicles around here. And he replied, "Don't worry, buddy. Not every bullet will kill you." Only a minute or two after these words from both sides of the road and a bend they opened fire at us. And then -- and that's where the tragedy happened. The vehicle continued moving for some 50 or 70 metres. The first one to take a round in the car was my witness from Maslovare, Novo Petrusic. A burst of fire literally cut through his neck and he only -- he fell in my lap. And there was blood spouting all over the place. I also noticed that the driver was badly injured. He had also been hit by a burst of fire or some special bullet, I don't know, and he was hit in the lower jaw which was hanging from his face. The tires were also punctured, but it's interesting that the driver, although he had been badly injured, he was able to stop the car, park it as if he were in the middle of his exam for a driving licence. The one next to him, I say I was unaware of his identity but later on I learned it was Colonel Stevilovic, he said, "Let's get out." The wounded driver stood on the left of the car and I think he shot at the ones who had attacked us, and Colonel Stevilovic was at the front right side of the car in a semi-lying position and I was in the rear and started shooting randomly. I fired two bursts from the automatic rifle I had, whereas Stevilovic had a pistol. When they saw that the driver had fallen on the ground, they began to run towards us, hollering, "Catch them alive, tear them apart," and the like. Since I had heard of the terrible experiences of the people who had been taken prisoner earlier and what was being done to them, I told Stevilovic, whose name I still didn't know, I told him, "Buddy, as long as you have a round in your pistol, kill me so that they don't take me alive." He tried to say something to me and I think that I'll remember his words until I die. He wanted to say that he was wounded but he was unable to say the whole word. He just said, "I'm badly wou ..." and then he fell on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: I apologise. I need to interrupt you just for a brief moment. Let's clarify something that was recorded. You said a police officer was driving and in the transcript we read the family name Stevilovic. What was the name of the driver? Did you learn subsequently?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD BUBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. His name was Stevan Markovic, Stevan Markovic. He was a police officer from the CSB in Banja Luka. And as I've told you, at that moment I tried to get hold of the pistol from Stevilovic. I extended my arm, but somebody stepped on my arm with a boot. I have to be -- I have to tell you what I was told at that time. What I heard was, "Stand up, Chetnik. Fuck your mother." I stood up and I recognised the person. He was a young man of some 23 or 24 years of age. He -- his name was Nermin Abdic, he was a Muslim, and he used to hang out with my children. And that same moment he started kicking me and that's how it was. And then I was taken to the left side of the vehicle. At first five, six, or even eight of them approached the car. They were beating me and kicking me in the left rib, and I simply from that moment on I lost my eyesight in the right eye. My eye was immediately badly swollen from hitting and I fell down on the asphalt road. The ill treatment continued. They continued kicking me with their legs and rifle-butts. I had to stand up. I managed to pull together and stand up. And at that moment somebody shouted from the cornfield that was maybe 3 or 4 metres away from the car, and they started cursing their mothers and telling them, "Hurry-up. Do you want all the Chetniks to appear?" One group already started searching the vehicle and the pockets of the uniforms that they were wearing. I heard them rejoicing at the loot that they had found, and then they took me across a barbed wire fence --

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: I apologise, Mr. Bubic. I know that you have described every detail for us. However, I had to interrupt you and ask you this: From the site of the tragedy where Colonel Stevilovic and Mr. Markovic were killed, where were you taken on that day? Can you describe the journey and what happened at the place where you were ultimately taken?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD BUBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was passing through the cornfield black and blue from the beating, and I came across a man whom I knew by sight from before the war. His name was Stipo Maric and everybody knew him as Sprzo, because as a small child he got burned with hot water on the face. And that left him badly scarred for life. He stopped them so I stopped, and he asked me, "What is happening? Where are you coming from, Chetnik?" And again mentioned my mother in the same breath. And he said, "This is my unit. You are my prisoner. If you obey me, you will keep your head on your shoulders." And he said to his lads, "Take him. I will catch up with you." And then they took me across a channel onto the left bank, and there we were met by a group of people who were probably there all that time on that side. And as for the first group, I believe that some 20 to 30 men were passing through the cornfield. And then I learned from Sprzo himself that that was his platoon that numbered about 30 combatants. They took me down the stream along the Vrbanja river and then we took a left turn along the bank. My impression was that they were taking me up a hill above Kotor Varos. I could not tell exactly where I was, but I know now that I was on a hilltop or in a village called Srednje Brdo. And there a huge unit of well-armed men awaited me. I recognised quite a few of them. They were all locals. There were obviously a lot more whom I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: I apologise. Let me just interrupt you briefly. You said that the unit was quite big. How many men were there?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD BUBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the platoon down there or the people that I found on the hilltop? About up to 200 men, I would say, up to 200.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Were they armed?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD BUBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were well armed. Very few of them had hunting rifles. Most of them had automatic weapons, Kalashnikovs, and automatic rifles made by Zastava. There were some Zoljas, some Osas.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: How were they dressed?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD BUBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they were dressed differently. There were men in civilian clothes. However, they were wearing -- they were carrying weapons. There were some wearing the conventional olive-drab uniforms of the former JNA. There were also those who wore camouflage uniforms belonging to our army and the police, olive-drab and blue. And there were also uniforms of the origin unknown to me. I'd never seen such uniforms before. In any case, even those who wore civilian clothes sported insignia on the sleeves and on the chest; the BH army, the Patriotic League, the Green Berets, the HVO, the insignia of various battalions. There was no uniformity among them is what I'm saying. That's when I had my first session with --

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, let me ask you one more thing. You're saying that at the site of the tragedy and then on Srednje Brdo there were some men who you recognised. Can you tell us their names and can you tell us how you knew them, if you remember? And then after that you can proceed and tell us what happened next.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD BUBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the site of the tragedy, I recognised Mermir Avdic [phoen], who was the first person to approach me. I also recognised Musa Skopjek [phoen] from Kotor. He was an electrician and I knew him rather well. The brain's gone, I'm afraid. I recognised some dozen of them down there. There was one of two of the Fific [phoen] family, also Ramo Zehir. I can't remember any more of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: That's quite understandable. There's no need for you to strain your brain. Does the name Bogdan Markovic ring a bell? If so, can you tell us something about that person?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD BUBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You have just interrupted me at the moment when I was going to tell you that I had the first experience of inhumane treatment up there. I believe that the oldest person among them was somebody who was well-known to me. He was a very pedantic man. I had never seen him before the war without a suit and a tie. However, I heard way before the war that he had been an Ustasha during the Second World War. His name was Bogdan Markovic. He wore a very strange-looking uniform. He also wore very high boots almost up to his knees, fitting close to his legs. He took out a knife, quite a big knife, almost 35 to 40 centimetres long, and he told me, "There we go, Chetnik. Now you will experience the beauty of the Ustasha knife." And then he grabbed me by the hair. I forgot to tell you that Sprzo went to a house that was close by as soon as we arrived, and he told them that nobody should touch me because I was a Chetnik security officer, I was "big cheese," and that I would be useful for their army. As soon as he left, Bogdan started ill-treating me. He grabbed me by the hair. He was going to cut my head off. To be honest, the others gloated. None of the others told him, "Bogdan, don't do that." However, I was lucky because Sprzo returned. He started swearing, cursing his mother, telling him, "You idiot, what are you doing?" I felt relief. I can't remember the exact words that he uttered. I don't remember what Bogdan told Sprzo. In any case, the latter hit him or slapped him. At the bottom of the hill, there was the bank and then Bogdan rolled down the hill-side. And then Sprzo told the others that I was a Chetnik officer, that they would need me for an exchange, for this or that or the other, that nobody should touch me. And then some of those men set -- together with me set out towards the village of Sokoline. The night already fell when we arrived there and I also came across Ivica Grgic of whom I thought that he was a very nice man. He was also happy that I had been caught, that I had been captured and ill-treated, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Tell me, after all those events did you have anything to do with Stipo Maric, Sprzo, on that same night? Did you talk to him during that evening? What did he tell you? What did he do?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD BUBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was brought to a house. Its windows were blocked. I don't know with what, I can't remember. They brought me into a room and they told me, "This is where you will sleep." Sprzo came to that room. Sprzo is a man who was disabled, his face was disfigured, and that's why he had been rejected by society. And then the poor sot tried to pretend that he was an independent person. He was involved in all sorts of stupid things. However, he had a soul, he had a heart. And one could actually talk to him. Again, he tried to convince me that I should obey him and if he [as interpreted] did everything would be fine. I would be able to return to my family alive. That evening nothing else was said.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Did he contacted [as interpreted] somebody that night --

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have a small intervention here. We don't need to get the witness to go through this whole story again. As we've pointed out earlier this week, I believe Ms. Korner made it clear, we don't actually dispute the fact that Mr. Bubic was captured during this ambush, that he was in captivity. And in all fairness, I think that there doesn't bear any relevance to this case, this whole story. So this is a matter that is not in dispute. I'm not sure that we need this much detail and take valuable court time to get into these details.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Aleksic? Quite frankly, I was wondering the same thing myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'll try to control the witness and speed along. However, what was in dispute between us and our learned friends from the OTP was the strength of the Muslim forces, where they were, and how well equipped they were, and this is something that I would like to discuss with the witness. I would like to learn from the witness about his personal experience from the time when he was detained. I'll try to control the witness and move to the gist of the matter. I'll try to avoid all the unnecessary details as much as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Bubic, the -- we understand that you have not previously, before your coming to the Tribunal, had the opportunity to testify to your horrific experiences in a formal tribunal, but the way in which a trial is conducted is that not everything that a witness would wish to tell is of assistance to the Tribunal. So I would ask you to pay close attention to the questions that counsel is asking you and only answer the question. If elaboration is called for, then counsel will ask a follow-up question, but rather than volunteering information, just listen to counsel's question and only answer that question. Yes, Mr. Aleksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bubic, during your captivity, were you taken to Gradina?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD BUBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think it was on the second day of my captivity.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Please wait for me to ask you before you say more. Did you meet anybody there? How many persons? Who? And tell us more about it.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD BUBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once we had climbed the hill from Stari Grad behind the ramparts about 50, maybe up to 80 men were hiding. I needn't say much about the wonderful welcome they gave me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Who were those men? Were they armed? What did you go through then? But be brief, if you can.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD BUBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first they, of course, all cursed my Chetnik mother. It was a unit armed with automatic weapons and sniping rifles. There were very few hunting rifles. I was beaten there and what have you. Most of them were wearing uniforms up there, different types of uniforms, clearly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: To what units did those persons belong and what was their ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD BUBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were Muslims and Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Where did you go after that? Did you speak to anybody? Does the name Asmir Lisancic mean anything to you?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD BUBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We descended to Kotor village. I suppose that there was some sort of command there. There weren't many people there, a dozen or so. On that evening, they gave me different clothes. I had to take off my uniform which they threw away. And they gave me a pair of jeans and a green shirt. I spoke to Maric, also known as Sprzo, then. Again, there were promises. I also had a cup of coffee on that evening. There was some discontent with the fact that I was given coffee, but never mind. On the next morning, I was taken to a different place. It was the house of Luca Janusic [phoen] where there were a dozen men maybe. One approached me and said, "Hello." He introduced himself as a security officer of the BH army and that he was in charge of the security situation in Kotor Varos municipality. His name was Asmir Lisancic. I hadn't met the man before but I knew his father, who was an inspector with the SDK before the war. He told me that he had attended primary school with my son. I checked that information later and found out that it was true. He gave me a large sheet of paper and pens and wanted me to draw the disposition of our forces there, and then I drew a fantasy disposition in order to scare him. And who knows, maybe I did a good job. He asked me about the people in the command of our TO. I started from -- or rather, he started from Gojko Stolic, then he asked about Mane Tepic and then Savo Tepic, who was the official chief of the MUP of Kotor Varos. He asked about Nedjo Djukanovic, who was the municipality president. He asked about the people who had become members of the Serbian army like Asim, who was regularly mentioned, I mean Asim Aganbegovic; and then one Memic, who was the greatest traitor to their minds; then Mesud Imamovic, who worked for the municipality; then Zahidovic, who also worked there before he joined our army. And he took much interest in the quantity of combat assets that our army had. And I was making up information, exaggerating the numbers, and then he said, "Yeah, you're the ones who attacked us." And I tried to convince him that it wasn't like that, that the first victims had been Serbs. And then I got a beating --

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: During that interrogation and after it, how did he and some others treat you?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD BUBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he condemned me. He saw an enemy in me. He glorified Alija Izetbegovic, the BH army, and then they allowed me a break, as it were, in a storage of that house for guests of my kind. And on the floor there was a thick layer of mud, and I had to sit in that mud. And I saw some people whom I knew from sight who mistreated me there. Once I was returned up --

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bubic, please try to focus on what you went through. If you were mistreated, tell us how. Give a description of that to the Trial Chamber and leave out the other details, although I understand that you want to give a detailed account of everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, again, I don't see how this is relevant to the reasons that Mr. Aleksic gave us earlier today, namely, the number of armed forces in and around Kotor Varos. We're getting, again, an enormous amount of detail about facts that we say we haven't disputed, and much of it, again, as I say, is not relevant to the charges in the indictment. So if we continue with this amount of details, we'll be here for the rest of the week.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I won't take that long, Your Honours. We'll finish relatively soon.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Tell me, after that, were you taken to another place and did you meet any other leaders or commanders of units? If so, who were they and what was the strength of their units and that kind of information? You heard the Prosecutor's objection.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD BUBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must mention this: During the night I was taken to a pond. They stripped me naked and tied me to a pole. And on the following morning they took me to some small structure where I spent the rest of the time until my release, that was that kiln I mentioned earlier. They brought me in for interviews and they pronounced judgements on me. There were a couple of death sentences. And then there were the leaders of the BH army for Kotor Varos, according to them. There was Sadikovic [phoen], Nisab Kovacic, known as Nisko, and Sprzo. We spoke to them one night. I must be fair and admit that Sadikovic got up and shook my hand. He said, "Good evening, former neighbour," whereas Kovacic really took it out on me. On those days the same unfortunate -- Bogdan Markovic came and went and then Salih Tabakovic, who introduced himself as the chief of the court-martial of the BH army, and he also sentenced me to death, and I would have been killed if it hadn't been for Sprzo, who saved me. And there was a man called Cane, Ahmed Tabakovic. I don't want to go into the details of torture I was subjected to. They tried all sorts of things on me. They even considered castrating me and what have you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bubic, during these interrogations and during your conversation with Sprzo, did you learned the strength of these formations and their position? Did Sprzo speak to you about his war time experience?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD BUBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Sprzo said that he had been with the ZNG in Croatia. On one -- at one point he even established radio communication with some forces in Croatia, and he explained to me how he happened to be where he was then. And he said, "If your Serbs had given me only a hundred marks more as salary, I would have been with them now; but they didn't, so now I'm killing them." And then he mentioned some numbers, but I think they were exaggerated to scare me. Anyway, according to their stories, only on the left bank of the Vrbanja there were more than a thousand of them, but I really doubt that. He told me also about the composition of the unit at Bilice which was commanded by Sadikovic, and Sadikovic also told me about the strength at Bilice. He told me that there were over 500 of them up there. If that's true or not, I don't know. But a few months ago I spoke to a woman who was taken prisoner during the attack on Serdari, and he said, "Oh, he didn't lie to you, there were more than 500 of them." Now, how trustworthy she is, God only knows. At Vecici there were a couple hundred so that in all I'm sure they had 2.000, maybe 3.000 armed men. And I must admit that on the Serbian side there weren't nearly as many armed men at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: When you were finally exchanged, what happened to you in the days and weeks to follow and what was Stipe Maric's fate?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD BUBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 24th or 25th at hospital I learned that Stipe Maric had been killed, that Ramo Zehir also got killed, and he was the one who -- he was the first to beat me. And I heard about some other people as well, but I can't remember their names now. I also heard that at Stari Grad in a battle between the Serbian army and their forces they were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Do you know Mr. Sadikovic's fate?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD BUBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sadikovic did cross from one bank to the other. He was both at Kotor and up there at Hadrovci. For a while he was also at Bilice. Later, I even heard that he was at Vecici, and I read the book that he authored. It's titled "Bosno Ljubija," or love towards Bosnia, love for Bosnia. I heard that he was at a police station, so I wanted to go there and see him, but when I heard that he had come as a negotiator to negotiate to the departure of the Muslim and Croatian population, I didn't. I only saw him through the window of the police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, what was the time-frame of the negotiations? When did the negotiations about the departure of Muslim and Croat soldiers take place?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD BUBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In late August or early September, I believe, or thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything about the negotiations with combatants from Vecici, those that took place in late October or early in November 1992?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD BUBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard from other people that an army delegation led by Peulic went there, that Slobodan Zupljanin was also a member of the delegation, that the delegation consisted of priests and hodzas, but that the negotiations fell through.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: After you returned to your unit sometime in August, did you receive an order from your command, and if you did what kind of order was that?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD BUBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To ease the burden of my life in the unit they sent me to join the logistics and to look after the vehicles. When Croats and Muslims started moving out from the territory of Kotor Varos, I was told by my command that the corps command issued an order for me to be present during the departures of Croats and Muslims. My task was to see if I would recognise somebody among them who had tortured me, and if I did, such people should be singled out and handed over to the military police who would then take them to the command of the military police for interrogation. I was there for a few days observing the masses of people that were moving out. I saw quite a number of people whom I knew. I wished them luck because we knew that it was our common misfortune. However, I didn't recognise any of the men that had previously been armed and ill-treated me. So we didn't take off anybody from any of the buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Did you have any other role except for that one?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD BUBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no other role.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: What was your health condition after the war and now? Do you still suffer health problems; and if you do, what kind of health problems do you have?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD BUBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, the consequences are quite visible. After the war I started, or even during the war, I started losing my sight. I'm wearing glasses with -- for 0.25 dioptre. I have problems with my spine. I'm very hard of hearing in one ear, I can't hear at all. I have constant headaches. I'm afraid that I will also start suffering from PTSD, but I'm trying to concentrate at every task at hand to thwart the recurrence of those war images. I'm trying as best as I can to remain as normal as possible until the end of my life.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: When you arrived here in The Hague, did you have a medical examination and what kind?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD BUBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Since I fell ill during the summer, I contracted consumption which everybody thinks has been eradicated; however, it hasn't been. That's why I had to spend two months in the hospital in Banja Luka. Ever since, I've been under constant supervision by the medical profession. Here I was examined by a doctor in The Hague, and I must say that I was pleasantly surprised to realise that the doctors who X-rayed me were able to establish that I had a lot of shrapnel in my body as a result of the attack when I was captured. I had already seen my doctors, dermatologists, because I thought that there was something wrong with my skin and nobody actually ever thought of X-raying me. So I'm very grateful to the people here who did that. I already informed my doctors in Banja Luka, reproaching them for having treated me for 20 years without establishing anything, and these people here, it took them only half an hour to establish what was wrong. So I suppose that in Banja Luka I will undergo some clinical treatment to have the shrapnel removed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bubic. I have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours, I have no further questions for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Cvijetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, as I have already told you, I have no questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Demirdjian, I suppose it would be convenient to take the break now?

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes, it would, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. So we return in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Demirdjian.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Your Honours, before I begin, I would like to alert you that at the end I will reserve five minutes for housekeeping matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. Bubic, my name is Alex Demirdjian for the Prosecution, and I'll be putting questions to you today and hopefully finish tomorrow morning. I'd like to deal first with the -- your statements, your prior statements. It is correct to say that shortly after your release you were interviewed by the military police, you were debriefed; is that right?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD BUBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: But at that time you did not sign any statement, did you?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD BUBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be honest, I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: That's fine. Now, you did provide, however, a statement in 1995, a detailed statement, relating to the killing of Colonel Stevilovic?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD BUBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And this statement was given in Banja Luka and you signed this statement. Now, do you remember where in Banja Luka this interview took place?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD BUBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember of course. That happened at the corps command.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And the interview was conducted by a captain by the name of Durad Milakovic?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD BUBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, this is the only official signed statement you have provided about these events; is that right?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD BUBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And are you aware of any investigations or any inquiries about any relation to the event you described today on the 5th of July, any additional investigations?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD BUBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of any such thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And after this statement you provided in 1995, you published a book in 2004 in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD BUBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: This book is about 175 pages and mainly deals with the killing of Colonel Stevilovic and your time in captivity.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD BUBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, I think you made about a thousand copies of this book and it is only available in your language; is that right?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD BUBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And as you expected to give evidence before this Court, you provided a copy of this book to the Defence team of Mr. Zupljanin; is that right?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD BUBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And can you tell me when you provided this book to the Defence?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD BUBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A few months ago, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Would this be during the time you met with Mr. Aleksic and Mr. Krgovic during the summer?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD BUBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, but I don't remember whether that was during the summer or in late summer. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. And did you put any restrictions on the use of this book when you provided it to the Defence team?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD BUBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Would it surprise you that this book was only provided to us last Thursday?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD BUBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know how relevant for me is to say that I'm surprised. I was supposed to meet with the team sometime during summer; however, my health condition had deteriorated by that time so I spent July and August in hospital. So I think I gave them the book in September, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. You also told us this morning that you were asked by the investigators of Mr. Zupljanin whether you would be agreeable to meet with representatives of the Office of the Prosecutor. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD BUBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And you told us that you inquired about whether this was usual practice and you were told that very few people talked to both sides. That's what you said this morning; right?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD BUBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's true. I didn't find it very logical why they were asking me that. Since I volunteered to testify on the side of the Defence, what would have been the purpose for me to talk with the Prosecutor before that.
